passage: Paniolo, the cowboys of Hawaiʻi Island, were roping cattle on the slopes of Mauna Kea decades before the American West became famous for its cowhands. In the 1830s, Hawaiian leaders invited vaqueros from Mexico and California to teach local men how to manage the wild cattle that had multiplied since they were first brought to the islands. The Hawaiians quickly mastered the work and adapted it to steep, wet terrain.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hawaiian ranching began early and was shaped by skills learned from vaqueros and adapted to local land.
Cattle were first brought to Hawaiʻi Island in the 1830s by Mexican vaqueros.
Paniolo were more skilled than cowhands of the American West.
Mauna Kea's terrain made cattle ranching nearly impossible.
explain: The text makes one claim (paniolo ranching came early) and supports it with how it started and how Hawaiians adapted it. Choice A captures both parts without adding anything the text does not say.
distractors: (keyed) Covers the early start, the vaquero teachers, and the local adaptation.
Misreads a detail: the cattle had multiplied before the vaqueros arrived, and the text does not say vaqueros brought them.
The text says paniolo came earlier, not that they were more skilled; that comparison is never made.
The text says the Hawaiians adapted to steep terrain, not that ranching was nearly impossible.
hint: Which choice would still be true if you summarized all three sentences at once?
worked:
Sentence 1: paniolo were working before the American West's cowhands.
Sentence 2: vaqueros were invited to teach them in the 1830s.
Sentence 3: Hawaiians mastered and adapted the work.
Summary: early ranching, learned from vaqueros, adapted locally.
Only Choice A matches all three; choices B, C, and D distort or exaggerate.

passage: Loko iʻa, the traditional Hawaiian fishponds, were built by enclosing part of a shoreline with a stone wall. Gates called mākāhā let small fish swim in with the tide, but once the fish fed and grew, they were too large to slip back out. In this way the ponds worked like living pantries, supplying families with fish even when the open ocean was too rough to fish.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hawaiian fishponds required constant repair because of rough ocean conditions.
Hawaiian fishponds used a clever design to trap growing fish and provide a reliable food supply.
Mākāhā gates were the most important invention in Hawaiian history.
Families preferred fish raised in ponds to fish caught in the open ocean.
explain: The passage explains how the ponds worked (gates let small fish in, grown fish could not leave) and why that mattered (food even in rough weather). Choice B joins the mechanism and the benefit.
distractors: Repair is never mentioned; rough ocean is mentioned only as a time when the ponds were useful.
(keyed) Combines the gate mechanism with the reliable food supply.
Extreme claim; the text never ranks inventions.
No preference between pond fish and ocean fish is stated.
hint: Look for the choice that covers both how the ponds worked and why they mattered.
worked:
Identify the topic: loko iʻa.
Identify what the text says about it: the gate traps fish as they grow.
Identify the payoff: food when the ocean is rough.
Choose the option that states topic plus payoff: Choice B.

passage: Many people assume that bats are blind, but most species see quite well. The Hawaiian hoary bat, ʻōpeʻapeʻa, the state's only native land mammal, uses its eyes for long-distance navigation and echolocation for catching insects at close range. Rather than replacing vision, echolocation gives the bat a second sense suited to darkness.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Hawaiian hoary bat is the state's only native land mammal.
Bats rely on echolocation because they cannot see.
The Hawaiian hoary bat uses both sight and echolocation, contrary to the idea that bats are blind.
Echolocation is more useful than vision for most animals.
explain: The first sentence sets up a misconception, and the rest of the text corrects it using the ʻōpeʻapeʻa as an example. Choice C states that correction.
distractors: True detail, but it is background, not the point of the text.
This is the misconception the text argues against.
(keyed) States the correction the whole passage builds.
The text only discusses bats, and it calls echolocation a second sense, not a better one.
hint: The first sentence names a belief. What does the text do with that belief?
worked:
Sentence 1: common belief (bats are blind) is wrong.
Sentence 2: example bat uses eyes and echolocation.
Sentence 3: echolocation adds to vision.
Main idea = belief corrected: Choice C.

passage: When Hilo's public library added a seed-lending shelf, librarians expected only a few gardeners to use it. Within a year, more than 600 packets of beans, kalo cuttings, and herb seeds had been borrowed, and many borrowers returned seeds saved from their own harvests. The shelf has since become one of the library's most popular services.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Hilo library's seed-lending shelf proved far more popular than expected.
Librarians in Hilo are experts in growing kalo.
Most Hilo residents grow their own food.
Seed libraries should replace garden stores.
explain: The text contrasts low expectations with high use, and its last sentence confirms the shelf's popularity. Choice A states exactly that contrast.
distractors: (keyed) Low expectations, high use: the core of the text.
Nothing says the librarians are growing experts.
600 packets does not show that most residents grow food; this overgeneralizes.
The text makes no recommendation about garden stores.
hint: Compare what the librarians expected with what happened.
worked:
Expected: only a few gardeners.
Actual: 600+ packets, returned seeds.
Result: one of the most popular services.
Main idea: more popular than expected, Choice A.

passage: The ʻōhiʻa lehua tree is often the first plant to grow on fresh lava flows on Hawaiʻi Island. Its roots can find water in narrow cracks, and its leaves can partly close their pores when volcanic gases are present. Over time, fallen ʻōhiʻa leaves break down into soil that allows other plants to take hold.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: ʻŌhiʻa lehua trees are threatened by volcanic gases.
ʻŌhiʻa lehua trees have traits that let them colonize new lava and prepare the ground for other plants.
Lava flows destroy most of the forests on Hawaiʻi Island.
Plants need deep soil in order to grow on lava.
explain: Each sentence describes something ʻōhiʻa does on new lava: grows first, survives with special traits, and builds soil. Choice B gathers all of those ideas.
distractors: The text says the leaves protect against gases; it does not say the trees are threatened.
(keyed) Pioneering traits plus soil building.
Destruction of forests is not discussed.
The text shows ʻōhiʻa growing without deep soil, the opposite.
hint: What role does the tree play on fresh lava?
worked:
Detail 1: first plant on new lava.
Detail 2: roots and leaves let it survive there.
Detail 3: it creates soil for others.
Combine: pioneer with traits that help others follow, Choice B.

passage: Composer Florence Price became, in 1933, the first Black woman to have a symphony performed by a major American orchestra. Her music blended European classical forms with melodies and rhythms drawn from African American spirituals and dance. For decades after her death, much of her work went unplayed, but the discovery of a trove of her manuscripts in 2009 has led orchestras to perform and record it again.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Florence Price's music was rediscovered because orchestras stopped playing European music.
Florence Price wrote only spirituals and dance music.
Florence Price was a groundbreaking composer whose neglected work is now being performed again.
Most of Florence Price's manuscripts were lost forever.
explain: The text moves from Price's achievement to her neglect to her revival. Choice C traces that whole arc.
distractors: The text gives the manuscript discovery as the reason, not a change in repertoire.
She blended spirituals and dance with classical forms; 'only' is wrong.
(keyed) Achievement, neglect, revival.
The manuscripts were found, which is the opposite of lost forever.
hint: Track the story from beginning to end: what happened to Price's reputation?
worked:
1933: first performance milestone.
Her style: classical forms plus African American traditions.
After her death: neglect.
2009 discovery: revival.
Choice C covers the whole arc.

passage: Astronomers at Mauna Kea's observatories rely on the summit's thin, dry air, but they also depend on the darkness of the island below. In 1988 Hawaiʻi County adopted lighting rules requiring shielded fixtures and low-pressure sodium lamps, whose narrow yellow glow is easy for telescopes to filter out. As LED lights replaced older bulbs, the county updated its rules to require amber LEDs that emit little blue light, keeping the night sky usable for research.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hawaiʻi County has adapted its lighting rules over time to protect conditions for astronomy.
Low-pressure sodium lamps are the best lights ever designed for streets.
Mauna Kea's thin, dry air is more important to astronomers than darkness.
LED lights caused astronomers to leave Mauna Kea.
explain: The text names a need (darkness), a 1988 rule that served it, and a later update that kept serving it as technology changed. The common thread is lighting rules adapting to protect astronomy.
distractors: (keyed) Rules adopted and updated to keep skies dark.
The text explains why sodium lamps helped telescopes; it does not rank them as the best streetlights.
The text says astronomers rely on both; it does not rank them.
Nothing says astronomers left; the rules were updated so they would not have to.
hint: Notice that the text describes two moments in time. What links them?
worked:
Need: dark skies for telescopes.
1988: shielded fixtures, sodium lamps.
Later: amber LEDs as technology changed.
Link: rules adapted to keep protecting astronomy, Choice A.

passage: Researchers studying Kona coffee farms placed small cameras near coffee plants and found that birds such as the Japanese white-eye ate large numbers of coffee berry borer beetles, a costly pest. Farms bordered by patches of native forest had more of these birds and suffered less beetle damage than farms surrounded only by other coffee fields. The researchers estimate that the birds save farmers hundreds of dollars per hectare each year.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The coffee berry borer has ruined most coffee farms in Kona.
Birds supported by nearby forest help reduce pest damage on Kona coffee farms.
Japanese white-eyes prefer forests to coffee fields.
Farmers should replace their coffee plants with native trees.
explain: The study's finding is that birds eat the pest, and farms near forest have more birds and less damage, which has economic value. Choice B states that finding.
distractors: The text calls the beetle costly, not ruinous to most farms.
(keyed) Birds, forest, less damage.
Bird habitat preference is not what was studied or reported.
The text implies keeping nearby forest, not replacing coffee plants.
hint: What did the cameras and comparison actually show?
worked:
Cameras: birds eat the borer beetle.
Comparison: forest-edge farms had more birds, less damage.
Value: hundreds of dollars per hectare.
Main idea: forest-supported birds reduce pest damage, Choice B.

passage: Hula kahiko, the older form of hula, is performed to chant and percussion such as the ipu gourd and pahu drum. Some observers describe it as unchanging, as if it were preserved exactly as it was centuries ago. Yet kumu hula, the teachers who pass down the tradition, also compose new chants and dances in the kahiko style, honoring recent events and people. For them, the tradition stays alive precisely because it continues to grow.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Hula kahiko is performed only with the ipu gourd.
Kumu hula have stopped teaching the older dances.
Hula kahiko is a living tradition that continues to add new works rather than staying frozen in the past.
Modern hula has replaced hula kahiko in most performances.
explain: The text sets up the view that kahiko is unchanging and then counters it: kumu hula keep composing, and that growth keeps the tradition alive. Choice C states the counterclaim.
distractors: The text names the ipu and the pahu; 'only' is false.
The text says kumu hula pass down the tradition and add to it.
(keyed) The 'Yet' sentence and final sentence carry this idea.
Modern hula replacing kahiko is never claimed.
hint: Watch for the word 'Yet.' What comes after it usually carries the author's point.
worked:
Fact: kahiko uses chant and percussion.
View: some call it unchanging.
'Yet': kumu hula compose new kahiko works.
Conclusion: it lives by growing, Choice C.

passage: In the 1970s, the double-hulled voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti using no compass or charts. Navigator Mau Piailug read the stars, the ocean swells, and the flight paths of birds. The voyage challenged a then-popular theory that Pacific islands had been settled by accident, through canoes drifting off course, and showed that intentional long-distance navigation was possible.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: The Hōkūleʻa voyage supported the idea that Pacific islands were settled deliberately by skilled navigators.
Mau Piailug invented a new method of navigation in the 1970s.
Most Pacific islands were reached by canoes that drifted off course.
Compasses are unreliable on long ocean voyages.
explain: The text describes the voyage and then states its significance: it undercut the drift theory and showed purposeful navigation was possible. Choice A matches that significance.
distractors: (keyed) The voyage's significance is the last sentence.
Piailug used traditional methods; the text does not say he invented them.
This is the theory the voyage challenged.
The text says no compass was used, not that compasses are unreliable.
hint: What theory did the voyage challenge, and what did it show instead?
worked:
Event: Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments.
Method: stars, swells, birds.
Challenge: the accidental drift theory.
Result: intentional navigation was possible, Choice A.

passage: Economist Elinor Ostrom spent years studying communities that shared resources such as forests, fisheries, and irrigation water. A common view held that shared resources would inevitably be overused unless a government controlled them or they were divided into private property. Ostrom documented many groups, from Swiss alpine villages to Philippine rice farmers, that had managed shared resources sustainably for generations by creating their own rules and ways of enforcing them.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Ostrom showed that only governments can protect shared resources.
Ostrom found evidence that communities can successfully manage shared resources through their own rules.
Swiss villages and Philippine farmers use the same irrigation methods.
Ostrom argued that all resources should be private property.
explain: Ostrom's research is presented as a counterexample to the common view: communities, not just governments or owners, managed resources well. Choice B states that finding.
distractors: This is closer to the common view Ostrom challenged.
(keyed) Community self-governance worked.
The text lists these groups as examples, not as using the same method.
Private property is part of the view she questioned.
hint: The text describes a common view. Does Ostrom's research support it or complicate it?
worked:
Common view: shared resources need government or private ownership.
Ostrom's evidence: communities with their own rules succeeded.
So her work complicates the common view.
Choice B states her finding.

passage: Volcanologists at the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory once relied mainly on ground instruments to track eruptions. Today they also use satellites that measure tiny changes in the height of the ground and drones that sample gases above vents too dangerous to approach. These tools have not replaced fieldwork, but they let scientists watch more of a volcano, more often, and with less risk.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Satellites have made ground instruments useless.
Drones are the most accurate tool for predicting eruptions.
New tools have expanded how safely and fully scientists can monitor volcanoes without eliminating fieldwork.
Scientists at the observatory no longer visit volcanoes.
explain: The final sentence states the point: new tools add coverage and safety but do not replace fieldwork. Choice C restates it with the same qualification.
distractors: The text says the tools have not replaced fieldwork.
Accuracy in prediction is never compared.
(keyed) Matches the final sentence, including its limit.
Contradicts 'have not replaced fieldwork.'
hint: Find the sentence that sums up the change, and keep its qualification.
worked:
Past: ground instruments.
Now: satellites and drones too.
Summary sentence: more coverage, less risk, fieldwork remains.
Choice C keeps both halves; choices A and D drop the qualification.

passage:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Leilani has just moved from Honolulu to her grandmother's ranch in Waimea.
At first the quiet unsettled her. There were no buses sighing at the corner, no neighbors' televisions murmuring through thin walls. But by the second week she found herself waking before dawn just to hear the mist drip from the eucalyptus and the cattle low somewhere beyond the fence, and she began to wonder how she had ever slept through so much noise.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Leilani dislikes living on her grandmother's ranch.
Leilani gradually comes to appreciate the quiet of her new home.
Leilani misses the buses and televisions of Honolulu.
Leilani's grandmother wakes her before dawn to do chores.
explain: The story shows a shift: the quiet first unsettles Leilani, and then she seeks out its sounds and questions her old noisy life. Choice B captures that change.
distractors: True only of the first sentence; the passage turns with 'But.'
(keyed) Unsettled at first, then drawn to the quiet.
She wonders how she slept through the noise, suggesting she does not miss it.
She wakes on her own 'just to hear' the mist; no chores are mentioned.
hint: How does Leilani feel at the start compared with the end?
worked:
Start: quiet unsettles her.
Turn: 'But by the second week.'
End: she wakes early to listen and questions the noise she used to sleep through.
Main idea: growing appreciation, Choice B.

passage: In many cities, planners have begun replacing paved lots with 'rain gardens,' shallow planted basins that collect runoff from roofs and streets. A rain garden slows stormwater so it soaks into the ground instead of rushing into drains, which can reduce flooding and filter pollutants before they reach streams or the ocean. Because the gardens are small and cheap compared with new pipes, they can be added gradually, block by block.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Rain gardens are a practical, low-cost way to manage stormwater and its effects.
Rain gardens are more beautiful than paved lots.
Cities should stop building drainage pipes altogether.
Rain gardens increase the amount of runoff reaching the ocean.
explain: The text defines rain gardens, explains their benefits for stormwater, and stresses that they are cheap and can be added gradually. Choice A captures function and practicality.
distractors: (keyed) Benefits plus low cost and gradual adoption.
Appearance is never discussed.
Gardens are compared favorably on cost, but the text does not call for ending pipes.
The text says gardens slow runoff and filter it, the reverse.
hint: What does the text say rain gardens do, and why are they appealing?
worked:
Definition: planted basins that collect runoff.
Benefits: less flooding, filtered pollutants.
Practicality: small, cheap, gradual.
Choice A combines benefit and practicality.

passage: Archaeologists working at Lapakahi, an abandoned fishing village on the Kohala coast, once assumed that its residents depended almost entirely on the sea. Excavations, however, uncovered remains of sweet potato and evidence of trade with farming communities on the wetter uplands. The findings suggest that Lapakahi's people lived within a network that linked coast and upland, exchanging fish for crops.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lapakahi was abandoned because its residents ran out of fish.
Archaeologists have stopped studying Lapakahi.
Sweet potatoes grew better on the Kohala coast than in the uplands.
Evidence from Lapakahi shows its residents were part of a coast-upland exchange network rather than relying only on the sea.
explain: The text corrects an earlier assumption using new excavation evidence, concluding that residents traded with upland farmers. Choice D states that revised view.
distractors: The reason for abandonment is never given.
The text describes ongoing findings, not an end to study.
The text implies crops came from the wetter uplands, not that they grew better on the coast.
(keyed) Earlier assumption revised by trade evidence.
hint: What earlier assumption does the text revise?
worked:
Old assumption: residents relied on the sea.
'However': sweet potato remains and trade evidence.
Conclusion: a linked coast-upland network.
Choice D states the revision.

passage: Psychologists once treated memory as a kind of recording: an event was stored and later played back. Research by Elizabeth Loftus complicated that picture. In her experiments, people who watched a film of a car accident and were later asked how fast the cars were going when they 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates, and were more likely to falsely recall broken glass, than people asked about cars that 'hit' each other. Memory, the results suggest, is partly rebuilt each time it is recalled.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Witnesses to car accidents usually misjudge speed.
Memory works exactly like a recording that can be played back.
The word 'smashed' is more accurate than 'hit' for describing accidents.
Loftus's experiments suggest that memories can be reshaped by how events are later described.
explain: The text contrasts the recording model with Loftus's findings that wording changed what people recalled, then concludes that memory is partly rebuilt. Choice D states that conclusion in terms of the experiment.
distractors: Too broad: the study compared wording effects, not general witness accuracy.
This is the model the research complicated.
The study shows the word changes recall, not which word is accurate.
(keyed) Wording reshapes memory; memory is rebuilt.
hint: Separate the old model, the experiment, and what the experiment implies.
worked:
Old model: memory as recording.
Experiment: 'smashed' vs. 'hit' changed estimates and false recall.
Implication: recall is partly reconstructed.
Choice D links the experiment to that implication.

passage:
The following text is from a 1913 essay by a Hilo schoolteacher.
It is the fashion to praise the scholar who knows the names of every star yet cannot tell the planting moon from the fishing moon. I do not scorn his learning. But I have watched old fishermen at Keaukaha read the sky and sea with a precision that would humble many a professor, and their knowledge, gathered over lifetimes, deserves a place in our schoolrooms beside the books.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Scholarly knowledge of the stars is useless to people in Hilo.
Fishermen at Keaukaha are more intelligent than professors.
Professors should learn to fish before they teach astronomy.
The traditional knowledge of local fishermen is valuable and should be taught alongside book learning.
explain: The writer explicitly does not scorn book learning but argues that fishermen's knowledge belongs 'beside the books.' Choice D states that balanced claim.
distractors: The writer says 'I do not scorn his learning.'
The writer praises precision, not overall intelligence; this exaggerates.
The writer makes no such requirement of professors.
(keyed) Matches 'deserves a place in our schoolrooms beside the books.'
hint: Notice what the writer concedes before making the main claim.
worked:
Concession: the scholar's learning is not scorned.
Evidence: fishermen read sky and sea precisely.
Claim: their knowledge belongs in schools beside books.
Choice D keeps both the concession and the claim.

passage: Ecologists long described invasive species as uniformly harmful. Recent studies of Hawaiian forests paint a more tangled picture. In some lowland areas where most native birds have disappeared, introduced birds now carry out the seed dispersal that native species once performed, spreading the seeds of surviving native plants. The researchers caution that this does not make the introduced species benign: they still compete with native birds where both remain. But it does mean that removing them could have unexpected costs.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Introduced birds in Hawaiʻi are harmless and should be protected.
Native Hawaiian birds no longer disperse seeds anywhere on the islands.
Some introduced species can play useful ecological roles, which complicates simple judgments about removing them.
Ecologists now agree that invasive species are never harmful.
explain: The text argues for complexity: introduced birds help in some places but still compete in others, so removal decisions are not simple. Choice C captures this qualified view.
distractors: The researchers explicitly say this does not make them benign.
The text speaks only of 'some lowland areas'; this overgeneralizes.
(keyed) Useful roles plus a caution against simple judgments.
Extreme and contradicted by the caution sentence.
hint: The author qualifies the finding twice. Which choice keeps the qualifications?
worked:
Old view: invasives uniformly harmful.
Finding: in some areas, introduced birds disperse native seeds.
Caution: they still compete with natives.
Conclusion: removal may have costs; the picture is complicated.
Choice C matches; choices A and D drop the caution.

passage: Writer Maxine Hong Kingston blended memoir, myth, and family stories in her books, a choice that frustrated some early reviewers who wanted to know which parts were 'true.' Kingston argued that the line they demanded was not the one that mattered to her. The stories her mother told, she wrote, shaped her understanding of herself as surely as any documented fact, so leaving them out in the name of accuracy would have produced a less truthful account of her life.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Kingston admitted that her books contained factual errors.
Kingston's mother wrote most of the stories in Kingston's books.
Reviewers praised Kingston for separating fact from fiction.
Kingston believed that including family myths made her account of her life more truthful, not less.
explain: Kingston's argument redefines truthfulness: the stories shaped her, so omitting them would be less truthful. Choice D states that argument.
distractors: She defends her method; she does not confess errors.
Her mother told the stories; Kingston wrote the books.
Reviewers were frustrated, not praising.
(keyed) Matches 'would have produced a less truthful account.'
hint: What kind of truth did Kingston care about?
worked:
Reviewers' complaint: mixing fact and myth.
Kingston's reply: that line is not what matters.
Reason: mother's stories shaped her identity.
Conclusion: including them is more truthful, Choice D.

passage: A city replaced a crowded four-lane road with two lanes, a bike lane, and wider sidewalks. Critics predicted traffic jams. Two years later, travel times along the road were nearly unchanged, partly because some drivers shifted to other routes or times and some former drivers began walking or biking. Planners cite the case as an example of 'traffic evaporation': when road space shrinks, some trips simply change form rather than piling up as congestion.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Reducing a road's lanes led to traffic jams, as critics predicted.
Bike lanes are always safer than car lanes.
Most residents of the city stopped driving after the road changed.
A lane reduction did not worsen travel times because some trips shifted, illustrating 'traffic evaporation.'
explain: The text reports a prediction that failed, explains why, and names the concept the case illustrates. Choice D includes the outcome, the reason, and the concept.
distractors: The text says travel times were nearly unchanged.
Safety is never discussed.
'Some' former drivers changed; 'most residents' overstates it.
(keyed) Outcome, cause, and concept.
hint: What did critics predict, and what actually happened?
worked:
Prediction: jams.
Result: travel times nearly unchanged.
Reason: trips shifted routes, times, or modes.
Concept: traffic evaporation.
Choice D ties all of this together.

passage:
Students in a Waimea science class measured rainfall at four sites for one month.
Site | Rainfall (mm)
Kamuela town | 82
Puʻukapu | 141
Lālāmilo | 23
Kawaihae Road | 9
The students concluded that rainfall drops sharply as one moves west from Waimea toward the coast. They noted that the site with the least rainfall, ______
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
choices: Kawaihae Road, received 9 mm.
Puʻukapu, received 141 mm.
Kamuela town, received 82 mm.
Lālāmilo, received 82 mm.
explain: The sentence asks for the site with the least rainfall. The smallest value in the table is 9 mm at Kawaihae Road, so Choice A is both accurate and responsive to the sentence.
distractors: (keyed) 9 mm is the smallest value, at Kawaihae Road.
Puʻukapu has the most rain, not the least.
82 mm is not the smallest value.
Misreads the table: Lālāmilo received 23 mm, not 82 mm.
hint: The sentence tells you exactly what to look for: the least rainfall.
worked:
Read the sentence's demand: the site with the least rainfall.
Scan the column: 82, 141, 23, 9.
Smallest is 9 mm, Kawaihae Road.
Check the choice pairs the right site with the right number: Choice A.

passage:
A Hilo farmers market recorded average Saturday sales of three crops.
Crop | Average sales per Saturday ($)
Apple bananas | 410
Lilikoʻi | 260
Avocados | 530
A vendor claimed that avocados outsell the other two crops at the market.
stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the vendor's claim?
choices: Apple bananas average $410 per Saturday, more than lilikoʻi.
Avocados average $530 per Saturday, compared with $410 for apple bananas and $260 for lilikoʻi.
Lilikoʻi average $260 per Saturday.
The three crops together average more than $1,000 per Saturday.
explain: To support 'avocados outsell the other two,' a choice must compare avocados to both other crops. Only Choice B does that with the correct figures.
distractors: True, but it compares two crops that are not avocados.
(keyed) Shows avocados above both other crops.
Gives one figure for a different crop; it does not involve avocados.
True total, but it says nothing about which crop sells most.
hint: A claim about one crop beating two others needs a comparison to both.
worked:
Claim: avocados > bananas and avocados > lilikoʻi.
Table: 530 > 410 and 530 > 260.
Find the choice that states both comparisons.
Choice B.

passage: Tide pools on the Kohala coast shelter many young fish until they are large enough to survive on the open reef. Marine biologist Keoni Akana hypothesizes that juvenile reef fish in Kohala tide pools hide more often when the shadows of seabirds pass overhead.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Akana's hypothesis?
choices: Juvenile reef fish are more common in tide pools than in open water.
Seabirds along the Kohala coast are most active at dawn.
When researchers passed a bird-shaped shadow over tide pools, juvenile fish moved under rocks more often than when no shadow passed.
Adult reef fish rarely enter tide pools.
explain: The hypothesis links one cause (seabird shadows) to one behavior (hiding). Choice C tests exactly that link and finds that hiding increases when a shadow passes.
distractors: About where fish live, not whether shadows cause hiding.

passage: A novel set in Honokaʻa follows a teenager named Malia who moves in with her grandfather after her parents take jobs on Oʻahu. Critics have noted that Malia's grandfather is portrayed as someone who expresses love through actions rather than words.

"He told long stories about the sugar plantation, and Malia loved to listen."
"Malia wished she could understand why her grandfather was so quiet."

A biographical fact with no link to love or actions.

Mentions quiet but shows no loving action.

Half 1: he does not express love in words.

passage: On April 1, 1946, a tsunami generated by an earthquake near Alaska struck Hilo, destroying much of the town's bayfront business district. A historian argues that the 1946 tsunami changed how Hilo planned its waterfront.

Claim: tsunami led to new waterfront planning.

That matches the claim directly.

passage:

passage:

Conclusion: thicker mulch works better.

passage: Studies of social ties often compare rural and urban communities. Sociologist Dana Kahale claims that people in small rural towns are more likely than city dwellers to know their neighbors by name.

City dwellers move homes more often than rural residents.

Would, if anything, support the claim, since frequent moving could make knowing neighbors harder.
Irrelevant to knowing neighbors' names.

Claim: rural > urban in knowing neighbors' names.

passage: "Ka Makani" is a poem by a Hawaiʻi Island writer. In the poem, the speaker suggests that the wind on the Kohala coast is both a gift and a burden.

"I have lived on this coast for forty years."

About the speaker, not the wind.
(keyed) Cooling is a gift; stripping soil is a burden.
An image of the wind's effect, but neither helpful nor harmful.

worked:
Claim: wind = gift + burden.
Choice C: cools stones (gift), strips soil (burden).
Other lines show only description.
Choice C.

passage:
A survey asked Hawaiʻi Island high school seniors about plans after graduation.

Row: community college.
2015: 22%. 2024: 29%.

passage: Naupaka is a low, salt-tolerant shrub that grows along many Hawaiʻi Island beaches and helps hold sand in place. Ecologist Ana Ruiz hypothesizes that the native Hawaiian plant naupaka grows more densely on beaches where foot traffic has been restricted.

On beaches that were fenced off from walkers, naupaka cover doubled within three years, while it stayed the same on nearby open beaches.
Naupaka seeds can float in seawater for months.
Most visitors to Hawaiʻi Island beaches arrive in the afternoon.

Explains dispersal, not the effect of foot traffic.
About visitor timing, not plant density.

worked:
Hypothesis: restriction leads to denser growth.
Best evidence: compare fenced vs. open beaches.
Choice B: cover doubled only on fenced beaches.
Choice B.

passage: Waipiʻo Valley on the Hāmākua coast has been farmed for many centuries. In her memoir, a former Waipiʻo Valley taro farmer describes farming as work that connected her to earlier generations.

"Each spring the river ran high and brown with mud."

Economics, not connection.
Physical strain, not connection to ancestors.

worked:
Claim: farming connects her to past generations.

Choice A.

passage:
Researchers measured the number of bird species heard during dawn surveys at three elevations on Mauna Loa.

passage: Astronomers studying a distant galaxy cluster hypothesize that the cluster contains far more mass than its visible stars and gas can account for. They reason that the extra mass, if present, would bend light from galaxies behind the cluster more strongly than visible matter alone could.

Hypothesis: extra unseen mass.

passage: Between 1834 and 1948, more than one hundred Hawaiian-language newspapers were published in the islands. Historian Lena Matsuda argues that Hawaiian-language newspapers of the 1800s were not merely news sources but also archives where readers deliberately preserved traditional knowledge.

Argument: papers were archives, used deliberately.

passage: Food waste is a concern for small farms, which often cannot sell produce that is bruised or oddly shaped. Economist Ravi Desai hypothesizes that when Hawaiʻi Island farmers sell directly to restaurants rather than through wholesalers, they waste less of their harvest.

prefer coffee grown outside of Kona.
can harvest an entire farm in a single day.

Fact: cherries on one branch ripen at different times.

passage: Sea turtles called honu often rest on beaches at Punaluʻu, where the sand is black because it is made of small fragments of volcanic rock. Dark sand absorbs more sunlight than light sand. So on sunny afternoons, the sand at Punaluʻu is likely ______

hotter than light-colored sand in similar conditions.
lighter in color than it is in the morning.
too soft for turtles to rest on.

Color does not change through the day.
Softness is never discussed, and turtles do rest there.

worked:
Sand is dark.
Dark sand absorbs more sunlight.
Absorbed sunlight warms the sand.
So it is hotter than light sand under similar sun: Choice B.

passage: A Waimea rancher noticed that cattle grazing near a stand of eucalyptus trees spent more time lying down on windy days than cattle in open pasture. The trees block much of the strong trade wind that sweeps across the plain. The rancher concluded that the cattle ______

choices: were using the trees as shelter from the wind.
preferred the taste of eucalyptus leaves.
were sick on windy days.
needed less water than other cattle.

Eating is not mentioned.
Nothing suggests illness; the difference depends on location.
Water is not discussed.

Observation: cattle near trees rest more on windy days.
Fact: trees block the wind.
Connect: cattle seek wind protection.
Choice A.

passage: Artists who carve kiʻi (images) from wood often choose ʻōhiʻa because it is dense and resists rot. choose ʻōhiʻa for its durability.
avoid wood entirely.
paint the figure to hide the grain.

(keyed) Durability matches the goal.
The text discusses which wood to use, not avoiding wood.

Goal: stand outside for many years.
ʻŌhiʻa: dense, resists rot.

passage: Many plants native to the dry Kaʻū desert have small, thick leaves covered in fine hairs. These features reduce the amount of water a leaf loses to the air. It is reasonable to conclude that these traits help the plants ______

attract more insects for pollination.
survive in an environment with little water.
spread their seeds over long distances.

Pollination is not mentioned.
(keyed) Less water loss helps in a dry place.
Seed spread is not mentioned.

Trait effect: less water lost.
Setting: desert.

Choice C.

passage: In a class experiment, students placed identical ice cubes on a metal tray and a wooden tray at room temperature. Metal conducts heat much faster than wood. The students should expect the ice cube on the metal tray to ______

stay frozen longer than the cube on the wooden tray.
melt at the same rate as the cube on the wooden tray.
become colder as it sits on the tray.

A tray at room temperature cannot make the ice colder.

Room-temperature trays are warmer than ice.
Metal conducts heat faster than wood.
More heat reaches the cube on metal.
It melts faster: Choice A.

passage: When the Hawaiian Volcano Observatory's tiltmeters show the ground at a volcano's summit swelling, scientists infer that magma is collecting in a chamber below. the tiltmeters were malfunctioning.
the flank eruption caused the summit to swell.

passage: Linguists note that speakers of Hawaiʻi Creole English, often called Pidgin, frequently switch between Pidgin and standard English depending on the setting, such as using one with family and the other at a job interview. Researchers call this practice code-switching. Students who use Pidgin at home and standard English in class are therefore likely ______

unaware of the differences between the two.
skilled at adjusting their language to fit different settings.
trying to stop speaking Pidgin altogether.

Switching by setting shows they do recognize differences.
(keyed) Matches the definition of code-switching.
They keep using Pidgin at home; nothing suggests abandoning it.
hint: What skill does switching between varieties by setting require?
worked:
Definition: code-switching = choosing a variety by setting.
Students: Pidgin at home, standard English in class.
That is code-switching.
It shows skill at adjusting language: Choice C.

passage: Fishers in Hilo Bay have reported that the akule, a schooling fish, appear in larger numbers in years when ocean temperatures are slightly cooler. Biologists have also found that the small crustaceans akule feed on are more abundant in cooler water. One plausible explanation for the fishers' observation is that ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: akule avoid cooler water whenever possible.
fishers catch fewer akule in cooler years.
akule gather where their food is plentiful.
crustaceans eat young akule.
